title: Hypoglycemia: Treat the Low Before It Becomes a Brain Emergency
bottomLine: A glucose below 70 mg/dL is clinically important even when symptoms are mild. If the patient is awake and can swallow, give the facility-approved fast-acting glucose treatment and recheck; if severe neuroglycopenia, seizure, or inability to swallow is present, use IV dextrose or glucagon per emergency order/protocol and protect the airway.
recognize: Adrenergic: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety
Neuroglycopenic: confusion, behavior change, visual disturbance, weakness, seizure, unconsciousness
Older adults and patients with recurrent hypoglycemia may have few warning symptoms
assess: Check bedside glucose promptly when symptoms occur
Assess ability to swallow, mental status, recent insulin/secretagogue dose, meal intake, exercise, renal function, alcohol, and illness
Recheck glucose after treatment using the protocol and identify why the low occurred
actions: Conscious and safe to swallow: give measured rapid carbohydrate per protocol
Unable to swallow/severe: activate emergency pathway and give ordered glucagon or IV dextrose
After recovery, provide longer-acting carbohydrate/meal when appropriate and prevent recurrence
diagnostics: Bedside glucose guides immediate treatment; do not delay treatment of a symptomatic severe low while waiting for a laboratory glucose
medicationSafety: Insulin and sulfonylureas are common medication causes
Long-acting insulin or long-acting secretagogue effects can outlast initial correction, so recurrence monitoring matters
Beta blockers may blunt adrenergic warning symptoms
redFlags: Hypoglycemia after a long-acting drug with renal impairment
teaching: Carry rapid glucose, know personal symptoms, check glucose before driving when at risk, and ensure glucagon access/training when prescribed
Teach meal/insulin timing and sick-day/exercise adjustments from the established plan
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN treats hypoglycemia using orders/protocols, reassesses response, and reports recurrent or unexplained episodes. Independent insulin-regimen redesign is not assumed.
examTrap: Giving orange juice to an unconscious patient or walking away after the first normal recheck without addressing recurrence risk.
oneLinePearl: Low glucose threatens the brain—treat, recheck, prevent the next drop.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Insulin Administration: Match the Insulin to the Glucose, Meal, and Patient
bottomLine: Before insulin, verify the correct insulin, dose, route, current glucose, meal/feeding status, and patient-specific hold or correction parameters. The most dangerous routine error is a mismatch between active insulin and available carbohydrate or an incorrect insulin product/dose.
recognize: Rapid/short-acting insulin has meal timing implications
Basal insulin controls background needs and is not interchangeable with mealtime insulin
Concentrated insulin products create high-alert dose/device risk
assess: Check glucose and review nutrition status before prandial/correction insulin
Verify insulin product/concentration and dose; use independent double-checks where policy requires
Assess potassium when IV insulin or hyperglycemic-crisis protocols require it
actions: Coordinate mealtime insulin with food availability
Use the prescribed correction scale rather than inventing a dose
Rotate subcutaneous sites while keeping technique consistent
Monitor response and hypoglycemia
diagnostics: A1C reflects longer-term glycemia but does not tell you whether today's scheduled insulin is safe to give without considering current glucose and intake
medicationSafety: Do not mix glargine/detemir/degludec with other insulins
Regular insulin is the conventional insulin used IV in DKA/HHS protocols; IV insulin requires intensive monitoring
Insulin lowers potassium by shifting it into cells
redFlags: Patient NPO but prandial dose still scheduled without clarification
Potassium too low for ordered IV insulin protocol
Pump failure with rising ketones in type 1 diabetes
teaching: Demonstrate pen/syringe technique, site rotation, storage, hypoglycemia treatment, and timing with meals
Never share insulin pens even if the needle is changed
scopeAndDelegation: Insulin administration is within PN/LVN scope in many settings but must follow state/facility policy, competency, and explicit orders. Dose adjustment outside an approved scale/protocol requires clarification.
examTrap: Giving rapid-acting insulin because it is scheduled even though the meal tray is delayed and the patient cannot eat.
oneLinePearl: Insulin safety is a three-way match: right insulin, right glucose, right nutrition.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: DKA: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, and the Closing Gap
bottomLine: DKA is ketoacidosis from insulin deficiency, not simply 'very high glucose.' Initial care restores circulation with prescribed fluids, verifies potassium, gives IV insulin per protocol when safe, replaces electrolytes, treats the precipitant, and follows resolution of acidosis/ketosis—not glucose alone.
recognize: Polyuria/polydipsia, dehydration, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, weakness, altered mentation
DKA can occur with glucose below the traditional very-high range, especially with SGLT2 inhibitors or pregnancy
Total-body potassium is depleted even when initial serum potassium is normal/high
assess: Vitals/perfusion, mental status, hydration, respiratory pattern, glucose, intake/output
Trend potassium, bicarbonate/pH, anion gap or ketone marker, renal function, magnesium/phosphate as ordered
Look for infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI, medication trigger, or other precipitant
actions: Start ordered isotonic fluid resuscitation and monitor response
Verify potassium before/during IV insulin per protocol
Administer IV insulin and electrolyte replacement as ordered
Add dextrose to fluids at the protocol threshold so insulin can continue clearing ketosis while preventing hypoglycemia
diagnostics: DKA diagnosis depends on hyperglycemia/diabetes plus ketosis and metabolic acidosis; serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is useful when available
Glucose may normalize before ketoacidosis resolves
medicationSafety: IV insulin can rapidly lower potassium and glucose
SGLT2 inhibitors can be associated with euglycemic DKA; report compatible symptoms even if glucose is not extreme
redFlags: Cerebral edema concern, especially in children
teaching: Never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes solely because oral intake is poor unless specifically directed
Use sick-day glucose/ketone monitoring and seek care for persistent vomiting, ketones, dehydration, or DKA symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: DKA IV-insulin and electrolyte protocols may require higher-acuity staffing; PN/LVN participation depends on state/facility policy. Universal PN responsibilities are trend recognition, accurate protocol execution when authorized, and immediate reporting of potassium, glucose, rhythm, or neurologic deterioration.
examTrap: Stopping the insulin infusion as soon as the glucose reaches a near-normal value while the ketoacidosis is still unresolved.
oneLinePearl: DKA ends when ketosis/acidosis resolves—not when glucose merely looks better.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: HHS: Extreme Dehydration and Hyperosmolality
bottomLine: HHS is dominated by profound hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration with little or no major ketoacidosis. Fluid replacement and careful electrolyte/osmolality monitoring are central; neurologic status may worsen if shifts are too rapid or the patient remains severely dehydrated.
recognize: Marked polyuria/polydipsia followed by severe dehydration
Weakness, confusion, focal neurologic findings, seizures, coma
Often occurs in older adults with type 2 diabetes during infection, missed treatment, dehydration, or medication stress
assess: Perfusion, neuro status, hydration, glucose, urine output, cardiac/renal comorbidity
Trend sodium/corrected sodium, potassium, renal function, osmolality, and glucose according to protocol
Monitor for fluid overload in frail/heart/renal patients
actions: Administer ordered IV fluids and electrolyte replacement
Give insulin according to the HHS protocol after initial fluid/potassium considerations
Treat the precipitating cause and prevent VTE/pressure injury as ordered
diagnostics: HHS typically has high effective osmolality with severe hyperglycemia and minimal ketosis/acidosis compared with DKA
Neurologic symptoms can mimic stroke; evaluate both rather than assuming all deficits are caused by glucose
medicationSafety: Insulin and fluids can shift potassium and osmolality; frequent monitoring is essential
Avoid overly rapid correction beyond the prescribed protocol
teaching: Hydration, sick-day glucose monitoring, medication access/adherence, and early treatment of infection reduce recurrence risk
scopeAndDelegation: HHS often requires high-acuity protocol care. PN/LVN participation in IV insulin/electrolyte management is setting-dependent; monitor trends and escalate neurologic/hemodynamic changes immediately.
examTrap: Assuming an older confused patient with extreme glucose has 'just dementia' or treating the glucose number without addressing profound dehydration.
oneLinePearl: HHS is a dehydration/osmolality emergency as much as a glucose emergency.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Thyroid Storm: Hypermetabolic Collapse
bottomLine: Thyroid storm is severe decompensated thyrotoxicosis with hyperthermia, marked tachycardia/dysrhythmia, CNS change, and often GI/hepatic or heart-failure findings. Reduce physiologic stress, support cooling/oxygenation/circulation, give ordered antithyroid and adrenergic-control therapy in the correct sequence, and escalate immediately.
recognize: High fever, severe tachycardia/AF, agitation/delirium/seizure, vomiting/diarrhea, heart failure
Triggers include infection, surgery, trauma, abrupt antithyroid discontinuation, iodine exposure in susceptible patients
This is not uncomplicated anxiety with a fast pulse
assess: Continuous temperature, HR/rhythm, BP, mental status, heart failure signs, hydration
Review thyroid history/medications and precipitating illness
Trend glucose/electrolytes/liver and thyroid tests as ordered
actions: Emergency escalation, cooling, IV fluids when appropriate, oxygen/support
Administer ordered beta blockade when safe, thionamide, then iodine at the ordered interval after thionamide, plus corticosteroid/supportive therapy
Treat precipitating cause
diagnostics: Diagnosis is primarily clinical in a severely ill thyrotoxic patient; do not wait for all lab results before emergency treatment
Thyroid hormone tests confirm thyrotoxicosis but severity is clinical
medicationSafety: Propylthiouracil/methimazole can cause agranulocytosis/hepatotoxicity—report fever/sore throat or liver symptoms
Iodine is sequenced after thionamide in storm protocols
Beta blockers can worsen decompensated heart failure/shock in some patients and require careful selection
teaching: Do not abruptly stop antithyroid medication without medical guidance; report fever/sore throat promptly because of agranulocytosis risk
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers ordered emergency medications/support within scope and reports response. Sequencing and selection of antithyroid/iodine/beta-blocker therapy follow the emergency protocol/provider.
examTrap: Giving iodine before the ordered thionamide step in thyroid-storm treatment or treating agitation alone while missing hyperthermic cardiovascular collapse.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid storm = hot, fast, altered, and failing—emergency.

title: Myxedema Coma: Cold, Slow, and Hypoventilating
bottomLine: Myxedema coma is life-threatening severe hypothyroid decompensation: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatremia/hypoglycemia, and altered mental status. Support airway/ventilation, rewarm gently, give ordered IV thyroid hormone and stress-dose glucocorticoid, and treat the trigger.
recognize: Progressive lethargy/confusion/coma
Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension
Hypoventilation/CO2 retention, edema, delayed reflexes, hyponatremia/hypoglycemia
assess: Airway, respiratory rate/depth, SpO2 and blood gas when ordered, temperature, HR/rhythm, BP, glucose, neuro status
Review infection, cold exposure, sedatives/opioids, missed thyroid medication
Trend sodium and cardiac response during treatment
actions: Emergency airway/ventilatory support and monitored care
Passive/gentle rewarming rather than aggressive peripheral heating
Administer ordered IV thyroid hormone and glucocorticoid, treat infection/precipitant
diagnostics: TSH/free T4 support diagnosis but emergency treatment should not be delayed in a classic critically ill presentation
ABG may show hypoventilation; sodium/glucose abnormalities are common
medicationSafety: Sedatives/opioids can worsen hypoventilation
Thyroid replacement can stress the heart; monitor for ischemia/dysrhythmia
Glucocorticoid is often given until adrenal insufficiency is excluded
teaching: Long-term thyroid hormone adherence and follow-up prevent recurrence; do not stop therapy because symptoms improve
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes the syndrome, supports airway/warming/glucose care, administers ordered medications, and escalates; IV thyroid dosing decisions are provider-directed.
examTrap: Using aggressive heating blankets/hot baths that cause peripheral vasodilation and hemodynamic collapse in a severely hypothermic unstable patient.
oneLinePearl: Myxedema coma is the opposite storm: cold, slow, hypoventilating, altered.

title: Adrenal Crisis: Steroid Deficiency With Shock Risk
bottomLine: Adrenal crisis can cause hypotension/shock, weakness, vomiting/abdominal pain, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. Give emergency glucocorticoid and isotonic fluids as ordered, correct glucose/electrolyte problems, and treat the trigger—do not delay steroids for confirmatory testing in an unstable known/suspected crisis.
recognize: Known adrenal insufficiency plus infection, vomiting, surgery/trauma, or missed steroid
Abrupt withdrawal after prolonged systemic glucocorticoid exposure can precipitate adrenal insufficiency
Hypotension resistant to routine fluids/vasopressors may raise concern
assess: BP/perfusion, HR, mental status, glucose, volume status, nausea/vomiting
Trend sodium, potassium, renal function and ECG if hyperkalemia significant
Review steroid history and stress-dose plan
actions: Emergency IV/IM hydrocortisone or equivalent as ordered
Isotonic fluids and dextrose when indicated
Treat precipitating infection/illness and monitor response
diagnostics: Cortisol/ACTH may be drawn before steroids if it does not delay treatment
Electrolyte/glucose abnormalities support severity but are not required to act in shock
medicationSafety: Chronic glucocorticoids generally require tapering rather than abrupt cessation after significant exposure
Patients with adrenal insufficiency need stress-dose instructions for illness/procedures
teaching: Wear medical identification, carry emergency steroid when prescribed, understand sick-day/stress dosing, and seek urgent care if unable to keep oral steroids down
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers emergency steroid/fluids under order/protocol and monitors response. Do not withhold a time-critical ordered steroid because the cortisol result is pending.
examTrap: Stopping long-term prednisone abruptly or waiting for endocrine testing while the patient is hypotensive and deteriorating.
oneLinePearl: Adrenal crisis = shock risk + steroid now.

title: Systemic Corticosteroids: Helpful Drug, Predictable Risks
bottomLine: Longer or higher-dose systemic corticosteroid exposure can cause hyperglycemia, infection risk, hypertension/fluid effects, mood/sleep change, osteoporosis, myopathy, GI risk, eye effects, and adrenal suppression. Give exactly as prescribed, monitor predictable complications, and never teach abrupt discontinuation after suppressive therapy.
recognize: Cushingoid features, proximal weakness, bruising/thin skin, glucose elevation, edema, mood change, infection with muted fever
Adrenal suppression risk depends on dose/duration and individual factors
Steroid withdrawal can produce weakness, hypotension, nausea, and adrenal crisis
assess: Glucose, BP, weight/edema, infection signs, mood/sleep, bone/fall risk
Review NSAID/anticoagulant use and GI history
Monitor eye/bone/renal or electrolyte parameters as ordered for chronic therapy
actions: Administer with food when appropriate and at prescribed timing
Use infection precautions and report subtle infection
Follow taper exactly when one is ordered
Support bone-protection plan when prescribed
diagnostics: Glucose/A1C, bone density, eye exams, electrolytes, and other monitoring depend on duration/risk
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop suppressive systemic therapy
Live vaccines may be contraindicated at immunosuppressive doses; verify before administration
Steroids can raise glucose and may require temporary diabetes-treatment adjustment by the prescriber
teaching: Carry medication/steroid information, report infection, follow taper, maintain bone-health plan, and ask before vaccines/NSAIDs when on chronic high-dose therapy
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN monitors predictable adverse effects and reinforces taper/safety teaching. Dose taper design is prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Stopping prednisone abruptly because swelling and blood sugar are worsening rather than notifying the prescriber and following a safe taper/alternative plan.
oneLinePearl: Steroids suppress inflammation—and the adrenal axis.
sourceBasis: Endocrine Society glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency guidance

title: SIADH: Too Much Water for the Sodium
bottomLine: SIADH causes water retention and dilutional hypotonic hyponatremia. Neurologic symptoms determine urgency: headache/confusion can progress to seizure/coma. Track sodium, fluid balance, daily weight, and neuro status; follow fluid restriction and ordered sodium-directed therapy without correcting chronic hyponatremia too rapidly.
recognize: Low serum sodium/osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine in the right clinical context
Weight gain without major peripheral edema may occur
Neurologic severity relates to sodium level and speed of decline
assess: Neuro checks, seizure risk, intake/output, daily weight, serum sodium/osmolality
Review medications, CNS/pulmonary disease, malignancy, pain/nausea triggers
Confirm fluid-restriction adherence
actions: Implement prescribed fluid restriction
Seizure precautions for severe symptomatic hyponatremia
Administer ordered hypertonic saline or other therapy under close monitoring when indicated
diagnostics: Serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium support the diagnosis after excluding other causes
Frequent sodium checks are needed during active correction
medicationSafety: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia risks osmotic demyelination
Some antidepressants, anticonvulsants, and other drugs can contribute to SIADH
redFlags: Overly rapid sodium rise during treatment
teaching: Explain the exact fluid limit and include hidden fluids such as ice, soup, gelatin, and beverages as instructed
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN accurately measures intake/output, enforces fluid restriction, performs neuro reassessment, and reports sodium/neuro changes. Hypertonic saline administration may require higher-acuity RN/critical-care policy depending on setting.
examTrap: Encouraging oral fluids because the sodium is low; in SIADH the problem is excess free water, not simple sodium loss.
oneLinePearl: SIADH = water held in, sodium diluted, brain at risk.

title: Diabetes Insipidus: Free-Water Loss and Rising Sodium
bottomLine: Diabetes insipidus produces large volumes of dilute urine and can cause severe dehydration and hypernatremia. Trend urine output, urine concentration, sodium, weight, thirst/mental status, and hemodynamics; replace water and give desmopressin for central DI when ordered while avoiding overcorrection/water intoxication.
recognize: Polyuria with very dilute urine, polydipsia, dehydration
Rising sodium/osmolality can cause irritability, weakness, confusion, seizure
Central DI can follow pituitary surgery/head injury; nephrogenic DI does not respond normally to ADH
assess: Hourly or frequent urine output when acute, daily weight, BP/HR, mucous membranes, thirst, mental status
Trend sodium, serum/urine osmolality/specific gravity
After pituitary surgery, report abrupt high urine output promptly
actions: Replace fluids according to ordered route/rate
Administer desmopressin for central DI when ordered
Monitor response so treatment does not swing the patient into water excess/hyponatremia
diagnostics: Serum and urine osmolality patterns support DI; specialized testing determines central versus nephrogenic causes
Do not use one high urine-output hour alone without assessing fluids/diuretics/context
medicationSafety: Desmopressin can cause water retention/hyponatremia if intake/dose exceeds need
Lithium can cause nephrogenic DI and requires medication review
teaching: Maintain prescribed access to water, know desmopressin dosing, and report abrupt urine/thirst changes or headache/confusion suggesting water imbalance
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN measurement accuracy is critical: urine output and fluid balance guide urgent decisions. Medication/fluid adjustment outside protocol requires provider direction.
examTrap: Restricting fluids in a patient with DI because urine output is excessive.
oneLinePearl: DI = water out, sodium up; replace and monitor carefully.

title: Acute Hypocalcemia: Neuromuscular Irritability Can Become an Airway Problem
bottomLine: Acute hypocalcemia can cause perioral/finger tingling, cramps, tetany, hyperreflexia, seizures, laryngospasm, and QT prolongation. After thyroid/parathyroid surgery, new tingling or stridor is urgent: protect the airway, check ordered calcium, and prepare to give IV calcium for severe symptomatic hypocalcemia.
recognize: Paresthesias, muscle cramps/spasm, tetany
Chvostek/Trousseau signs can support neuromuscular irritability but are not the only assessment
Laryngospasm/stridor and seizure are emergencies
Low magnesium can make hypocalcemia harder to correct
assess: Airway/voice/stridor after neck surgery
Neuro/muscular symptoms and seizure risk
ECG/QT and ordered calcium, albumin/ionized calcium, magnesium, phosphate
actions: Emergency airway support for laryngospasm/stridor
Administer IV calcium as ordered for severe symptomatic cases with cardiac monitoring
Correct magnesium when ordered
Use seizure precautions when indicated
diagnostics: Ionized calcium reflects biologically active calcium; total calcium is influenced by albumin
PTH/vitamin D/renal tests help identify cause
medicationSafety: IV calcium can injure tissue and affect cardiac conduction; give through the prescribed route/rate with monitoring
Separate oral calcium from medications whose absorption it impairs according to instructions
teaching: Take calcium/vitamin D as prescribed and report tingling, cramping, voice/airway changes after neck surgery
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN identifies symptoms and supports ordered replacement; IV calcium administration may be restricted to certain settings/competencies.
examTrap: Treating tingling after thyroid surgery as anxiety without checking for evolving hypocalcemia and airway risk.
oneLinePearl: Post-thyroid tingling can precede tetany—stridor makes it an airway emergency.

title: Diabetes Sick-Day and Foot Safety: Prevent the Emergency Before It Starts
bottomLine: During illness, diabetes can destabilize even when intake is poor. Continue monitoring, follow the individualized medication/sick-day plan, maintain hydration if possible, check ketones when indicated, and seek urgent care for persistent vomiting, dehydration, ketones/DKA symptoms, severe hypoglycemia, or altered mental status. Foot care focuses on daily inspection and early treatment—not soaking or self-cutting lesions.
recognize: Illness can raise glucose through stress hormones and can also cause hypoglycemia if intake falls while medication continues
SGLT2-associated DKA can occur without extreme hyperglycemia
Neuropathy may hide foot trauma/ulcers
assess: Glucose/CGM trend, hydration, ability to keep fluids down, ketones when indicated, medication use, fever/infection symptoms
Inspect feet for breaks, blisters, redness, warmth, drainage, callus, color change; assess footwear
Report new ulcer/infection or ischemic findings promptly
actions: Follow the written sick-day plan and contact the diabetes team when thresholds are met
Do not independently stop essential basal insulin in type 1 diabetes
Protect foot wounds and obtain appropriate podiatry/wound/vascular care
diagnostics: Ketone testing is important for type 1 diabetes and selected high-risk patients during illness/hyperglycemia
A1C does not replace day-to-day glucose monitoring during acute illness
medicationSafety: Some diabetes drugs need temporary holding during dehydration, fasting, acute illness, or procedures; follow the specific current sick-day plan rather than a universal rule
SGLT2 inhibitors require DKA-risk education
teaching: Daily foot inspection, properly fitting shoes, no barefoot walking, no heating pads on insensate feet, and professional treatment of high-risk calluses/nails
Keep sick-day supplies, glucose/ketone testing access, rapid carbohydrate, and emergency contacts
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN reinforces the established diabetes self-management plan and reports unsafe trends/foot findings. Medication sick-day adjustments must follow the prescriber's plan/protocol.
examTrap: Telling a vomiting person with type 1 diabetes to stop all insulin until they can eat normally.
oneLinePearl: Sick day: monitor more, hydrate, protect insulin needs, watch ketones; foot care: inspect, protect, report early.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
